title: Hickson Compact Group 40

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Five galaxies crowd together in this Hubble image of Hickson Compact Group 40, released to mark the telescope's 32nd birthday. The group holds three spiral galaxies, an elliptical galaxy and a lens-shaped lenticular galaxy, about 300 million light-years away in the direction of Hydra.

The whole group could fit inside a region less than twice the diameter of the Milky Way's stellar disk. Such tight groupings occur in the hearts of huge galaxy clusters, but these galaxies sit isolated in their own patch of the universe. One possible explanation is a large amount of dark matter. Moving through a shared cloud of it, the galaxies would feel a drag from its gravity, lose energy and fall together.

In about 1 billion years they are expected to collide and merge into a giant elliptical galaxy. Nearly every member has a compact radio source at its core, which could point to supermassive black holes, and X-ray observations reveal plenty of hot gas between the galaxies, a sign of their gravitational interaction.

understand.summary: Hubble's WFC3 took this image. NASA shows F475W in blue, F606W in green, and F814W and F665N in red.
understand.eye: The colors are hues assigned to four filters, including the narrow F665N, so they are not exactly what an eye would see.

explore: Sky surveys have cataloged over 100 compact groups like this, and few are as densely packed as Hickson Compact Group 40. Such tight groups may have been more common in the early universe, where they may have fueled quasars. Paul Hickson of the University of British Columbia rediscovered the group while browsing Halton Arp's 1966 collection of peculiar galaxies.
